#582. Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two

Black holes are known for merging when two of them collide, but could the reverse ever happen? Could a single black hole somehow divide into two smaller ones? A new theoretical study suggests that this extraordinary possibility may not be entirely ruled out by physics, although the conditions required would be extreme.

The research, published in Physical Review D under the title "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," examines the physical laws that keep black holes intact and whether certain circumstances could allow them to break apart.

"In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen," says Francesco Sannino, co-author of the study and a professor of physics at University of Naples Federico II in Italy and Quantum Field Theory Center at University of Southern Denmark.

The research team also included Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a researcher with the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint CNRS and Sorbonne Université laboratory in Paris. Additional contributors were Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.

Why Black Holes Normally Cannot Split Apart

One of the biggest obstacles to a black hole splitting comes from thermodynamics, the branch of physics that governs how energy behaves and how physical systems change.

A central concept is entropy, which describes how many different microscopic arrangements a system can have while appearing unchanged from the outside. Black holes have entropy, and this property places important limits on what can happen to them.

For a black hole that is not rotating, dividing into two smaller black holes would reduce the total entropy. Such a decrease makes the process thermodynamically unfavorable, helping explain why black holes do not ordinarily break apart.

However, the researchers found that the situation could change dramatically when a black hole spins at an exceptionally high speed.

Extreme Rotation Could Allow Black Holes to Split

The team's calculations suggest that rapid rotation may create a narrow opening in the physical rules that normally prevent black holes from dividing. In principle, a sufficiently fast spinning black hole could overcome the usual thermodynamic restriction.

But there is another major obstacle. Even if a black hole could divide, the two resulting objects would need to move far enough apart to avoid immediately merging again.

"But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," says Francesco Sannino.

The study's unusual title refers to the shape that a black hole's boundary would trace through space and time if such a split occurred. This boundary, called the horizon, would begin as a single structure before separating into two distinct branches.

Viewed across time, the resulting shape would resemble a pair of trousers, with one upper section dividing into two "legs." This is the idea behind the term "pair-of-pants topologies."

Extra Dimensions Offer Another Possibility

The researchers also investigated more unusual scenarios involving theories in which space has additional dimensions beyond the three we experience in everyday life.

Physicists have already identified objects resembling black holes in some of these theoretical models that can become unstable and start breaking apart. These possibilities suggest that the familiar rules governing black holes may not apply in the same way under more exotic conditions.

In certain cases, splitting could even become thermodynamically favorable, especially when one of the two resulting black holes is much smaller than the other.

However, a process being allowed or favored by thermodynamics does not necessarily mean it will happen. Researchers still need to determine whether such fragmentation can physically occur and what conditions would make it possible.

Could Astronomers Detect a Black Hole Splitting?

The scientists are now working to better understand how likely these events might be. The answer may depend on aspects of gravity that go beyond Einstein's theory, making the problem especially challenging.

"We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein's theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers," says Francesco Sannino.

Although there is currently no confirmed observation of a black hole splitting, the possibility of detecting signals from tiny fragments offers a potential way to investigate the idea. Such evidence could provide valuable clues about the behavior of gravity under some of the most extreme conditions in the universe.

Sannino is the director of the Quantum Field Theory Center (ℏQTC), which is affiliated with the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science (IMADA) at the University of Southern Denmark. He is also affiliated with the Danish Institute for Advanced Study and the Department of Physics "Ettore Pancini" at the University of Naples Federico II. In addition, he serves as a visiting professor at Durham University.

#578. IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos

An enormous number of invisible particles are constantly traveling through Earth, passing through our bodies and continuing into space as though almost nothing stands in their way. Known as neutrinos, these mysterious particles are among the most difficult objects in the universe to detect. Yet scientists are finding ways to capture evidence of their passage, opening new opportunities to investigate the cosmos and its most extreme environments.

Neutrino research has played a remarkable role in modern physics. Discoveries involving these particles have contributed to five Nobel Prizes in Physics. This year, physicist Francis Halzen received the prestigious award "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

George Fuller, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of California San Diego, has studied nuclear physics, particle astrophysics, and cosmology for decades. He also collaborated with Halzen on an early scientific paper about IceCube. His expertise helps explain what makes neutrinos so unusual and why scientists built an enormous observatory deep within the Antarctic ice to study them.

Neutrinos belong to a group known as elementary particles, which scientists believe have no smaller components. They come in three varieties, called electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. Unlike electrically charged particles, neutrinos have no electric charge. They do have mass, but it is extraordinarily small, potentially around 10 million times less than the mass of an electron. Their exact masses remain unknown, as does the mechanism responsible for producing them.

Another remarkable characteristic is their ability to travel through matter with almost no resistance. Because neutrinos interact so rarely with other particles, they can cross vast distances at speeds approaching the speed of light.

Neutrinos originate from many different places, including the Sun, distant regions of space, and sources scientists have yet to identify. They are also astonishingly abundant. Estimates suggest the universe contains roughly 1089 neutrinos, equivalent to approximately one billion for every atom in existence.

"Neutrinos are truly ghost-like particles," stated Fuller. "It's hard to stop them. It's hard to catch them. How do we even know they exist or where they are?"

Ghost Particles That Pass Through Almost Anything

Despite their elusive nature, neutrinos occasionally interact with matter through a fundamental force known as the weak interaction. This force is approximately 20 orders of magnitude weaker than electromagnetism. Such interactions can cause neutrinos to scatter or be absorbed, providing scientists with a way to detect them. However, these events are so uncommon that observing them requires exceptionally sensitive equipment.

Their ability to move through dense material also makes neutrinos valuable messengers from otherwise inaccessible regions of the universe. They can escape from environments surrounding collapsing stars and black holes, carrying information that other forms of radiation might not reveal.

The scale of this invisible activity is staggering. Approximately 100 billion neutrinos pass through every square centimeter of your body each second, almost entirely unnoticed.

"Because the interaction is so weak, neutrinos can get through almost anything," said Fuller. "Light years of lead -- depending on their energy, they would go right through it."

How Scientists Learned to Detect Neutrinos

The search for neutrinos began long before technology existed to observe them. During the 1930s, physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed that an unknown particle might explain why energy appeared to be missing during certain forms of radioactive decay. He initially used a different name for the hypothetical particle (he called them "neutrons" at the time).

Pauli understood how difficult it would be to verify his idea. He famously acknowledged the problem by saying, "I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected."

For decades, neutrinos remained beyond the reach of experiments. That changed in 1956, when physicists Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines successfully detected them in an experiment known as "Project Poltergeist."

The breakthrough established that neutrinos were real, but detecting them remained an enormous challenge. Scientists needed increasingly sophisticated instruments to investigate the rarest and most energetic neutrinos arriving from space.

Why Antarctica Is Ideal for Hunting Cosmic Neutrinos

During the 1990s, Halzen recognized that the South Pole offered an extraordinary natural environment for neutrino research. Far below Antarctica's surface, immense volumes of ice are exceptionally clear, with relatively few bubbles or contaminants to interfere with the detection of faint flashes of light.

His vision eventually led to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a gigantic scientific instrument embedded within roughly one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice. To construct it, researchers drilled deep holes and lowered long strings of sensitive light detectors called photomultiplier tubes.

These instruments search for brief flashes of blue light produced through a phenomenon called Cherenkov radiation. The light appears when a neutrino interacts with matter in the ice and produces a charged particle traveling faster than light can move through that material.

By recording these flashes, researchers can identify evidence of neutrinos that would otherwise pass through Earth without leaving a detectable trace.

IceCube is particularly important for studying neutrinos that arrive from distant cosmic sources with extraordinarily high energies. Unlike the enormous quantities of relatively low-energy neutrinos produced by the Sun, these powerful cosmic visitors are extremely rare. The observatory detects only a few dozen of the most energetic examples each year.

When one of these neutrinos interacts with the ice, it can produce a rapidly moving electron or muon. A muon, for example, generates a cone of Cherenkov light as it travels through the ice. Scientists analyze the resulting pattern of light to estimate the neutrino's energy and reconstruct the direction from which it arrived.

For Fuller, these exceptionally energetic neutrinos are among IceCube's most exciting discoveries because their origins and the physical processes responsible for accelerating them remain poorly understood.

"Some ultra-high-energy neutrinos detected at IceCube have roughly 10 billion times the energy of a typical neutrino from the Sun. One detected by a similar experiment has an energy 200 times higher than that. We don't really know where that neutrino came from," he stated. "The fact that it got here at all may be saying something profound about the universe. In that sense, Halzen really is at the frontier of experimental fundamental particle physics."

Neutrinos Could Reveal Secrets of the Big Bang

The scientific effort to understand neutrinos extends far beyond Antarctica. Researchers at UC San Diego are also involved in another major observatory that could offer new insights into these elusive particles and the universe's earliest history.

Located high in Chile's Atacama Desert, the Simons Observatory is gathering information about the cosmic microwave background, the ancient radiation left over from the early universe. Often described as the oldest light in the cosmos, this radiation provides a valuable record of conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

UC San Diego helped establish the observatory, and Brian Keating, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the university, serves as its principal investigator.

Although the observatory primarily studies ancient light, its measurements can also reveal information about neutrinos from the earliest stages of cosmic history. The project could provide an enormous amount of new data related to these ancient particles, potentially offering insights that other experiments cannot obtain.

Fuller believes the anticipated observations could improve scientists' understanding of the Big Bang, the early evolution of the universe, and other fundamental questions about how the cosmos developed.

"Halzen's work, and the work of those he inspired with his vision, was foundational in giving humanity a new window on the universe and on the mysterious and notoriously slippery neutrino," he stated.

#577. Is it legit? How to tell if that website or social media account is a scam

There is a 30 percent chance this article is fake.

It's not, of course. I am a real reporter. These are real sources. You can trust me.

According to a recent study from Pew Research, around one-third of recent web content is AI-generated. Around 10 percent of ".com" sites now have AI's fingerprints on them. Fake news sources peddling misinformation or propaganda (commonly referred to as "pink slime") have long outnumbered real news publishers — and are continuing to multiply with the help of AI.

Even legit websites and social platforms can steer you toward misinformation, scams, and other online dangers. A platform built to keep you hooked to an endless feed, fed by engagement and seeking to capture your attention, is a recipe for bots, phishing, and disinformation campaigns. Social media "experts" — sometimes entirely AI-generated people, other times real humans with ulterior motives — are building followings in the millions. In this increasingly confusing environment, here's how to get to the truth.

"High quality misinformation and deception were largely the domain of nation-states and well resourced groups," explained Donnie Hasseltine, chief information security officer at Arkstone Defense. Now, anyone can fake a site, build a bot, or amplify a misleading claim in an instant.

In addition to a decline in platform moderation, access to increasingly sophisticated AI models, mainly through open source markets, has completely changed how information is published, explained Zohaib Ahmed, CEO of deepfake detector Resemble.AI.

Likened to the "Wild West" by Ahmed, bad actors now have access to a host of AI models and tools without built-in safeguards to prove or disprove authenticity. They can avoid automatic detection built into mainstream models like Claude or ChatGPT, uploading troves of user and site data to build sophisticated spoofs without alerting developers.

The technology has generated a ballooning market for affordable "scam kits." Such kits cover "everything from advertising to writing blog posts and content on social media, to how features are being built in the product, how video calls are being done and how images are being uploaded onto social media platforms," Ahmed said. With a few hundred dollars, scammers can spoof entire sites, make convincing log-in portals, and build natural-looking engagement that makes it feel more real.

It's not just relegated to pink slime, either. You may encounter "url hijackers" or "typosquatting" for instance. These webpages closely mimic URLs for reputable sites — including news sites like "abcnews.com.co" or known organizations like FIFA — banking on users not looking too close. Others may spoof sites where it's common to exchange money or place bets. These domains may siphon off your personal information or try to steal your money outright.

The same happens on social media sites and chatrooms: X accounts meant to look like real people, dodgy TikTok Shop links that take users off site, suspicious links dropped in gaming chats by players you thought were your friends.

"The traditional signals of authenticity are fading," explained Eyal Elazar, head of market intelligence for e-commerce security business Riskified. "Only a few years ago, verifying something online relied on recognizable visual or contextual cues: a weirdly spelled URL, pixelated image artifacts, a robotic cadence in a video, or the sheer logistical effort required to pull off a coordinated hoax. Today, AI can effortlessly clean up misspelled URLs, blurry images, and stiff video voices."

Because users are up against a modern world of AI-powered websites and bot accounts, they also need new advice for scouring through the muck.

The OG way to ensure you're on a legit site still works and is very simple: Check the URL.

First, look for the padlock icon or other indicator the browser has verified your connection. For Google Chrome users, select the menu icon to the left of the URL. You should see "Connection is secure."

Second, look for "https://" not "http://". The "s" designation means a site has been authenticated.

These security components are still essential components of the internet, explained Ron Kerbs, CEO of AI fraud prevention company Kidas.

Third, double-check the URL's spelling, says Ahmed. Keep an eye out for symbols in the place of letters and non-English characters masquerading as the English alphabet. Hover over a URL to see the full text.

If you're still unsure, search the URL on Google. You can also cross-reference URLs on Google's site status page or use an online URL scanning tool, Ahmed recommends.  The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Many mainstream browsers now include built-in safety checks that flag when a website doesn't meet these security parameters. Pay attention to them, and only follow through on visiting a site if you know its origins.

But bear in mind that social media accounts do not play by these rules, experts warn.

To verify an account is legit, start with the platform's own verification tools, like the classic check mark. Be sure to click through to the profile itself, not just how it appears on your feed. Many platforms allow custom characters in display names, which help users fake verified check marks on first glance. Other platforms, like X, let users buy verification, so use additional means to confirm those accounts.

Be on alert for AI-generated influencer content, too. Look for AI content labels in captions, comments, and on profiles. Use the tips below to see if they've skirted detection (many do).

A site or account may seem legit on the surface, but its content could be far from it. Basic security measures aren't prevention for misinformation or manipulative content posted to verified platforms, experts say.

"You close the door, someone gets in through the window," Kerbs said. Users should use multiple layers additional methods beyond URL scanning to verify that what they're looking at is real.

Traditional recommendations for vetting news sources, for example, include the SIFT method. It's an oft-referred to media literacy skill designed by misinformation researcher Mike Caufield and stands for:

Other news literacy groups, like the News Literacy Project, suggest a strategy of "zoning," or  categorizing content, including websites and social media accounts, by their purpose.

"Identify the type of information you are looking at and determine its purpose. Is it news that’s meant to inform you? Or an opinion that’s trying to persuade you? Or is it a paid ad that’s encouraging you to buy something?" said Chuck Salter, president and CEO of the News Literacy Project. Salter recommends online users zone first before making judgements about trust. "You need to understand the main intent."

Salter also recommends a fact-checking concept called "lateral reading," in which you verify a source by searching what others are saying about it.

This can be used to fact check social media accounts, too. Before resharing, check the algorithm. How do others feel about this page?

Methods like SIFT and zoning are fairly simple and very effective ways to spot misinformation. But we're up against platforms actively working to steal our attention span and keep us glued to their platforms. We are urged to use integrated generative AI tools intended to reduce friction, but which can reduce users' critical thinking, experts say. Young people are at particular risk, Salter explained, and often fail to properly "zone" content without help.

We may need to simplify our toolkit even further.

For one, never trust a screenshot, said Roei Sherman, senior director of research at cloud security firm Mitiga. A common way to spread misinformation, faked screenshots feed off of the attention economy: Get enough people to share the eye-grabbing headline or quote, and you'll convince a good amount of people it's true, especially if a generally reliable source is slapped on top.

Second rule of thumb: If a post feels like rage bait, it's probably rage bait. Scammers and propagandists stoke emotional responses to get your clicks, Rubinson explains. Try not to engage.

And lastly, if an account is asking you to leave the platform you're on, exercise caution. Fake accounts often steer users off of moderated platforms toward other websites with looser content guidelines or toward completely unregulated areas of the internet. It's why many social media giants, like TikTok, have specific rules against the promotion of off-platform sites.

If it's best to check a claim with multiple sources, it's even better to check the claim with an authority that makes fact-checking its job. Long before AI, these sites existed as nonpartisan sources for political claims. Now, they've expanded to cover just about anything going viral.

NewsGuard AI False Claims Monitor and Reality Check newsletter

Some cybersecurity experts recommend browser extensions that can automatically scan a page for AI-generated content and give an assessment of its trustworthiness. These are a good starting point, but like most detector tech, are not infallible, experts like Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, warn.

Resemble.AI Deepfake Detector: Scans all images, video, and audio and returns a verdict on whether or not AI was used. A free account includes four website scans per day.

NewsGuard: Provides a trust and reliability rating for news sites, based on nonpartisan criteria.

McAfee Web Advisor: The free version of the cybersecurity's fraud tool, Web Advisor scans for malicious sites, including hidden adware, spyware, and phishing scams.

#576. NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice

Located in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula, Vega Island has a particularly haunting appearance when viewed from above. Its rocky and icy features resemble a grinning skull seen from the side, seemingly gazing toward nearby Devil Island. But behind this unusual sight is a more serious story about the changing condition of Antarctica's glaciers.

NASA satellite images show the island during the beginning of Antarctic autumn and during spring. The images were captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.)

Several natural landmarks create the skull's distinctive appearance. A nunatak, which is a rocky peak rising above the surrounding ice, resembles an empty eye socket. A lateral moraine, a ridge of material left along the side of a glacier, outlines the mouth. Meanwhile, Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier forms what looks like the skull's lower jaw.

The two satellite views also reveal a striking difference in snow coverage. In March 2025, snow blanketed the icy terrain, consistent with March being the wettest month in the region. By October 2026, however, extensive sections of the island were free of snow, leaving darker glacier ice exposed.

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College explained that unusually warm conditions during the winter of 2026, especially in June, contributed to the unusually large areas of exposed ice observed in October. According to Pelto, the exposed surfaces on Vega Island and neighboring islands suggest that relatively little fresh snow accumulated over the winter. Some of that snow was also lost through sublimation, when ice turns directly into water vapor, and through strong winds that swept snow away.

“The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”

The lack of snow could have important consequences as Antarctica moves into its warmer months. Fresh snow reflects much of the sunlight that reaches it, while darker, exposed ice absorbs more solar energy. As daylight increases and temperatures rise, these darker surfaces are likely to warm more quickly, potentially speeding up glacier melting.

Even a modest amount of new snowfall could temporarily slow that process by covering the exposed ice.

“Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said.

Continued melting could also gradually transform the island's unsettling appearance. The same ice and rock formations that give Vega Island its skull shape are vulnerable to changes as the glaciers retreat.

“When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”

Scientists have been studying Vega Island's glaciers for decades, and satellite observations have played an important role in documenting their condition.

One of the earliest detailed surveys appeared in a 1982 study that used early Landsat satellite data, aerial photography, and topographic maps to examine the island's ice cover. Researchers identified four ice caps, along with rocky cliffs extending above the ice and glaciers flowing outward from the ice caps. Altogether, they documented 29 glaciers across Vega Island.

One of these, Devil's Bay Glacier, has been monitored in detail since the Antarctic summer of 1998-1999. Measurements collected over that period show an overall reduction in the glacier's mass.

The changes are not limited to Devil's Bay Glacier. Satellite observations spanning recent decades reveal that other glaciers on Vega Island have also lost ice, exposing increasing amounts of the underlying bedrock.

Long before satellites began monitoring its ice, Vega Island played an unexpected role in one of Antarctica's dramatic early exploration stories.

The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 traveled to the region to investigate the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife of the eastern Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding areas. What began as a scientific mission turned into a desperate struggle for survival.

During the expedition, the explorers became separated into three groups, each forced to endure the Antarctic winter in a different location. Their situation became even more dangerous when pack ice destroyed their ship, leaving them stranded in one of the world's most unforgiving environments.

Despite the ordeal, Vega Island eventually became the setting for a moment of hope. In spring 1903, two of the separated groups reunited at a location later named Cape Well-met, near what now resembles the “forehead” of the island's giant skull.

Not long afterward, an Argentinean expedition arrived and rescued the survivors, bringing their extraordinary Antarctic ordeal to an end.

Today, Vega Island remains a place where dramatic natural formations, a remarkable history of exploration, and the effects of a changing climate come together. Its ghostly skull may be one of Antarctica's most unusual sights, but the gradual transformation of the ice that shapes it tells an even more important story.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.

#574. Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features

At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.

All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.

A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.

In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.

The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.

“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”

Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.

“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.

Websites linked to the apps have revealed the network’s secrets and the scale that it operates on. Opening one of the apps’ websites will likely show an entirely black screen and no content. The only noticeable change is that the URL updates to include the word “risk.” But the websites host the hidden explicit deepfake layer that can be loaded in each app.

This web interface contains dozens of pornography deepfake video and image templates—with users able to upload images of people to be added to the sexual scenes. The interface allows the purchase of “diamonds” to generate images and links to other social media accounts where users can contact the developers with questions or complaints.

Also hidden in the websites’ code are details about the entire network. A JavaScript bundle that can easily be unpicked, researchers say, contains a list of all the domains and apps that have been created by the developers—including app package details, encryption keys, Facebook advertising trackers, and more.

“They contained this giant configuration list of other domains with different encryption keys,” says Maël Le Touz, a staff threat researcher at security firm Infoblox, who identified almost 500 linked domains. “They run the same code and they all reference one another.”

Bouchard’s analysis of when domains were registered found that the apps started to appear toward the end of 2025, with a spike during the spring of this year. At one point, around 30 nudify apps-websites were being registered each week, the researcher says, with 27 live on Google’s Play Store in September. These apps had been downloaded more than 350,000 times collectively and many were rated suitable for all age groups, Bouchard’s research says.

One of the most popular apps, called DiffAI, was created in December 2025 and has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store. A user review on Google’s Play Store stated: “This app contains templates for creating CSAM and other types of pornographic material. It performs no age verification.”

DiffAI was removed from the Play Store shortly before WIRED contacted Google about the network. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, though it had removed the majority of the apps ahead of being contacted. (Portions of the deepfake network were reported on by Danish journalists in September.)

Similarly, Apple removed 19 apps from its App Store, including pet photo app Viefur, after WIRED asked the company about the activity and shared associated domains. “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for our users, and nudification apps and other pornographic content are strictly prohibited,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema.

“We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them,” Dema says. “After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.” The company says it has suspended tens of thousands of apps for using these “bait-and-switch” tactics over the last year and recently updated its app store rules to further restrict “nudify” tools.

Central to the “nudify” network appears to be a host of Chinese developers whose identities seem to have been intentionally hidden. “It’s using exclusive Chinese hosting, the code is written in Chinese and has a lot of comments in Chinese,” Le Touz says, noting explicit videos in ads posted to Meta’s platforms promoting the apps contained watermarks from Chinese-language video editing software.

“These ads violate not just one, but several of Meta’s policies,” says Katie Paul, the director of the Tech Transparency Project, who first uncovered the ads showing deepfake explicit depictions of minors. “There is no question about what you are seeing, what the app is advertising,” she says. Paul says tech companies need to answer questions about where money generated from the apps goes and how those behind the nudification apps and services constantly seem to bypass their content moderation and safety systems.

KeLing Technology Limited appears to be a significant part of the operation. While the company’s website is little more than a shell, its name was listed as the contact details of the first website registered in the network. This website’s brand name also appeared as part of the contact details within the explicit deepfake template that was used in the apps. Bouchaud also identified an administration login page linked to the explicit deepfake interface that mentions “Keling.” And email addresses using the company’s domain appeared on at least one app that have been removed from app stores.

Towards the end of September, a notification sent to users of the explicit deepfake interface announced that a new AI model could be used—the model was called Veyra, with a tagline in the apps of “More real. More natural. More wild.” The homepage of a website called Veyra AI listed its contact email as a KeLing Technology address.

Meta says it banned KeLing Technology Limited from advertising in 2025 after it failed to “comply with a cease and desist letter.” (Meta declined to share the letter with WIRED citing legal reasons.) “We have strict rules against promoting nudify apps and work aggressively to keep this material off our services,” a Meta spokesperson says. Meta says that while KeLing Technology Limited has continued to try and advertise through other ways, it takes action against the ads when it becomes aware of them.

After WIRED shared the 400-plus domains with Meta, the spokesperson said they had shared more than 3,000 associated ads linked to them, two-thirds of which it had already removed from its systems. Meta later told WIRED it has taken action against 11,600 ad accounts, more than 4,700 business pages, 5,200 users, and 15,000 pages linked to the domains, blocking 209 apps from advertising on its platforms.

“The criminals behind them take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection—hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google's and Apple's app stores, with the ads' true intent revealed only after a click,” the spokesperson says.

As WIRED finished reporting this story, similar ads and apps continued to be published on the tech platforms.

On the first day of his farewell tour in China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged the German business community to act with confidence in the Chinese market.

"When you travel in China, you're amazed at how highly Germany and German technology are still valued here," he said in Hefei. "That's why we can act with confidence in these markets."

Steinmeier did not bring any companies with him to China as part of his delegation, as his final trip was intended to focus on culture and science.

Nevertheless, the first day of the trip in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, revolved primarily around the economy. Steinmeier visited the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC). About three years ago, Europe's largest automaker opened a research center for electric mobility there, which today employs 3,000 people.

Johannes Volkmann, a lawmaker accompanying Steinmeier in China, warned that the German economy must not "lose its leadership in innovation."

"I'm taking this call to action with me from here to do more to improve competitive conditions at home," he said, adding that Germany must avoid creating new dependencies "by allowing innovation and value creation to take place only outside Europe."

Steinmeier called for Europe to reposition itself and reorganize its economic instruments with its growing trade deficit with China in mind.

"The trade surplus that China is accumulating naturally causes us concern because the successful model of economic cooperation is becoming unbalanced," he said. "We must strive to ensure that economic cooperation does not come to an end, but that it continues — to the mutual benefit of both sides."

Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) in 2025. According to the Federal Statistical Office, China exported goods worth €170.6 billion to Germany, and German exports to China amounted to €81.3 billion.

Across the 27-member EU, the deficit amounted to almost €197 billion in the first half of 2026, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.

Additional reporting by Rosalia Romaniec in Hefei.

A German court denied a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who stands accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines.

Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial this month at the Hamburg state court, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure.

Prosecutors accuse him of being the ringleader of the destruction, considered one of Europe's biggest acts of post-World War II sabotage. He is alleged to have carried out the explosions together with six others.

His lawyers said the charges should be dismissed, arguing that, as a former soldier, Kuznietsov was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for national security reasons and could face severe penalties in Ukraine if he did. They argued that, under German law, anyone who cannot speak on his or her own behalf cannot be convicted.

The Hamburg court ruled Kuznietsov's defense was not limited under German law and that freedom to testify is not limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.

The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which brought Russian natural gas to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022.

The blasts also damaged the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never went into service. Germany suspended the pipeline's certification process shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Italian authorities detained Kuznietsov last year. He was publicly named in extradition proceedings that led to his transfer to Germany in November.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.

Markets were quick to take note of the announcement, and Mercedes shares dropped 3.4% in trading on Tuesday morning.

The move makes Mercedes the third big German carmaker to lower its outlook for 2026 after BMW and VW took similar steps.

Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kaellenius has called on German employees to work more without pay while also expanding manufacturing operations in Hungary, where he said costs are about 70% lower than in Germany.

Like many German automakers, Mercedes has faced weak sales in China. German carmakers have struggled in the world's largest car market with sluggish demand and increased competition from local manufacturers.

Mercedes also released third-quarter figures earlier than planned, which showed that the company generated just €172 million ($191 million) in free cash flow from its vehicle business, down on the €422 million forecast by financial market experts.

The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.

Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.

In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.

Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.

Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.

The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.

Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.

BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.

The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.

Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.

Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.

The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.

The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.

Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.

The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.

Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.

In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."

The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."

"We must assert our interests in an international environment shaped by renewed great-power rivalry," Merz said.

Neither the United States nor China is part of the CPTPP.

For his part, Wong said investment in Germany and Europe would continue.

"Many of our investors, including our sovereign wealth funds, have been investing in Germany for a long time," Wong said. "They will continue to invest because they are confident that, in the long term, Germany and Europe have potential."

#571. Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response

Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.

Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.

Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.

"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."

Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain

To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.

The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.

Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.

How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat

By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.

The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.

These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.

"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."

The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.

"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.

There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.

Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.

The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, and Jared Smith from the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine, and Diabetes and Obesity Research Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California. Additional contributors included Kay Jann of the USC Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California, and Ting Chow and Anny H. Xiang of the Department of Research and Evaluation at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in Pasadena, California.

Funding came from an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36] and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. Support for the REDCap database used in the research was provided by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].

Materials provided by Keck School of Medicine of USC. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#570. 4 Best Alexa Speakers I’ve Tested (2026)

Amazon started the smart speaker game, but finding the best Alexa speaker has only gotten harder as the company launches more and more devices. Amazon has the largest range of smart speakers and displays by a long shot, which can be overwhelming to dive into. It currently includes the Echo Dot Max, the Echo Studio (2nd Gen), the Echo Show 11, and the Echo Show 8 (4th Gen). But Amazon has plenty of older, cheaper models available, too.

If you're looking for something small and simple to control your home, either an Echo Dot ($80) or the Echo Dot Max ($120) is your best bet. The Dot Max has really impressive sound for its compact size and is my overall favorite Alexa speaker, but if you're only going to use it for voice commands rather than jam sessions, you can get away with the older, cheaper model, especially if you want to buy a few to place around your home. For anyone looking for a smart display, the Echo Show 11 ($250) is the best of Amazon's newest smart displays that come designed for Amazon’s updated assistant, Alexa+. The older third-generation Echo Show 8 ($150) is still a great value if you want something cheaper.

However, there are several new models out after Amazon's announcement on October 28, and I'll be updating this guide soon on whether the newest models outpace the old. In the meantime, read on to see which of the existing Echo speakers are our favorites. You can also learn more about Alexa+, and we've got guides on setting up your Echo speaker, creating Alexa routines, and the best tricks an Echo Show can do.

Updated November 2026: I've updated this guide with details about the new Echo speaker models announced, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Out of all of Amazon's latest smart speakers, one landed on top for me: the Echo Dot Max. It's still a similarly sized speaker to past Dot models (though this model is slightly taller at 4.27 inches while the older one was 3.9 inches), but it has much better sound than ever before, putting it on a level with the Echo (4th Gen) we previously recommended. I was really impressed with the sound quality and volume for such a small speaker. It also doesn't lack in bass like smaller speakers usually do. Amazon is no longer selling the plain Echo, which was last updated in 2020, so the Echo Dot Max is really your only powerful sound option that isn't upward of $150.

While it still has the rounded design that was introduced in the 2020 Echo speakers, both the Echo Dot Max and new Echo Studio introduced a new design style with a front panel that looks like a dust cap, but instead houses the volume controls and the microphone mute button. There are also tap controls on the top to stop music, and it has a built-in smart home hub that was never before available in such a small speaker. It comes with Alexa+ right out of the box, but if you don't have a Prime membership, you'll only have a 30-day trial and then need to pay for either Prime or the Alexa+ $20 monthly fee (choose Prime).

The price on this model also rose recently, going from a base price of $100 to $120. It's not a huge increase, but a bummer to see, especially because that means sales on this device will also likely be on the higher end than in the past. It's on sale right now for $95, for example, but that's only $5 cheaper than the price it had just a week ago.

The fifth-generation Echo Dot is a few years old now, but it's still a great little speaker. It's got powerful, robust sound for its size, and it works great if you want Alexa handy on a bookshelf or on a small side table. It's got significantly improved bass from older models, which I really like for listening to music. It's one I always find myself setting up somewhere in my house, whether it's in my hallway so I can ask quick questions as I move through the house, or in my bedroom as an alarm clock.

It used to have some of the best sound you can get for the price, but Amazon did unfortunately raise the price on this speaker along with several other models. The base price used to be $50 and frequently on sale for around $30, but the base price is now $80 with its sale price going for $55. I wouldn't buy it if it's not on sale; it's not worth $80. Still, it's the best Amazon's got in the under-$100 category after the price hikes.

★ New 2026 Model: There's a new 6th-gen Echo Dot out, but it costs $100 now since it includes a smart home hub, Omnisense to sense the environment, the ability to extend your eero mesh Wi-Fi system, and improved bass. I'll be testing it soon, but while the new features are cool, it's frustrating to see the cheaper Echos get more and more expensive.

I'm surprised to say that out of Amazon's two newest Echo Show devices, the new Echo Show 11 ended up being my favorite over the fourth-gen Echo Show 8. I actually liked the larger screen, and it didn't feel ridiculously large like the Echo Show 15 does or the Echo Show 10 before it, but it helps that the base is much smaller on the Show 11 than the Show 10's rotating, Wall-E-esque base.

The Echo Show 11's screen is bright and crisp, and I loved how the landscape photo slideshows looked on it. There's a little side menu you can swipe to see things like your smart home favorites, and I found the sound quality immersive and more well-rounded than the new Show 8. Taylor Swift's “You're On Your Own, Kid” sounded beautifully dimensional, while “Opalite” didn't lose its bass like it did on the newer Show 8. It's got a 13-MP camera like we've seen on Show 8 models, and this larger display is one I'd be more likely to stream a show on compared to the smaller Show 8 and Show 5 sizes. If you're looking to get one of the newer displays, this is the superior option.

This smart display also rose in price due to Amazon's price hikes. It now has a base price of $250, when it used to be $220.

The Echo Show 8 has been our favorite smart display for Alexa for three generations in a row, and the 2023 model remains my preferred option of the Show 8 models, even though there's a newer version. The 8-inch screen is a good size for just about everything, from weather updates to recipes and video chats (thanks to the 13-MP camera), without being overly bulky.

The third-gen model has a smart home hub and spatial audio. I was also happier with the sound quality on this one compared with the newer fourth-gen Echo Show 8 ($200). While the fourth gen comes with Alexa+ right away and has an updated screen experience, the speaker is a little weaker and doesn't have the same bass and depth level to the songs as the third-gen version. The biggest irritation I have with the third-gen version is that Amazon will show lots of ads on it (along with other Echo Show devices), but there are some ways to get around that.

Not only do I love this model, but it hasn't risen in price like the newer Echo Show 8 and other Echo speakers I like, making it a better buy than ever.

While I wouldn't call these smart speakers my absolute favorites from Amazon, they have some excellent qualities that make them stand out among the vast lineup of Echo models.

The Echo Studio (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for sound quality. This is the second version of the Echo Studio to be our audiophile pick. The current version is a similar size to the old Echo (4th gen), but the musical power on this speaker is almost ridiculous. It filled my entire second floor's long great room with music, and I didn't even need to reach the highest level of volume to pull it off. Honestly, I'm almost afraid to use it at full blast. Not only was it loud, but clear and delivered a nice amount of bass, beautifully playing soft tones of Tracy Chapman's “Fast Car” and the piano riffs of “Dark Blue” by Jack's Mannequin with its three 1.5-inch drivers, plus a 3.75-inch woofer. The harmonizing of “What Is This Feeling?” by Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo sounded beautiful, too. If you're looking for big sound in an Alexa box, this is it. It's a similar size to the Apple HomePod, but I like the sound much better and it's cheaper, too. You'll also get a built-in smart home hub, spatial audio and Dolby Atmos, tap controls like the Echo Dot Max, and early access to Alexa+ right away.

The Echo Spot (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for bedside tables. The Echo Spot returned in 2024 after a few years of discontinuation, and it's a great little bedside companion thanks to its half-circle screen that displays the time, plus any alarms you have set are also visible under the main time. You can customize the clock with a couple of different color and face options, and the screen dims nicely when the lights are out to a gentle red that's easy to read without lighting up the room. I like asking for alarms set to my latest playlist or some lo-fi jams, and it's easy to set that up with a voice request. Unlike the Echo Shows, it doesn't have a distracting, constantly moving slideshow that would be annoying for the bedroom, nor does it display ads or have a built-in camera. (Nobody wants a rogue camera in their bedroom.) It does not have fantastic sound, but it's plenty loud for an alarm or casual listening while you get dressed in the morning.

The Echo Dot Kids (5th Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for kids. Do your kids really need their own Alexa speaker? That's up to you. This special edition of the Echo Dot is nearly identical to the fifth-gen Dot above, but it has easy-to-use parental controls that allow you to set time limits, filter explicit content, and review activity. The owl- or dragon-themed sphere comes with a year of Amazon Kids+, which includes thousands of Audible books and other special games and features. After that, you'll be charged $3 per month. Alexa can help your kids spell, play their favorite music, or—via another speaker in your house—remind them of dinner time.

There are a lot of Echo devices out there, and some third-party speakers that are Amazon Alexa–compatible. Here are other Alexa smart speakers we've tried and what we thought of them. Some of these speakers haven't increased in price like the models above, which might make them more appealing than before if you're looking to spend less.

Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) With Clock for $60: I like this version of the older Echo Dot that adds an LED clock to the front of the speaker, and was thrilled to see it in stock again last year. The LED clock can also display information like the weather when you ask Alexa questions. It's once again temporarily out of stock as of this writing, and has had spotty availability. Still, it's a good find when it's available. There is the new Echo Time ($200) out now too, which will likely eclipse the Dot With Clock in permanent availability.

Amazon Echo Hub for $180: The Amazon Echo Hub is similar to an Echo Show, but prioritizes smart home controls over entertainment. It's a slim device that feels a bit like a tablet, designed to be mounted on the wall (or placed on a separately purchased stand, which is how I used it) and used to control your smart home devices. It's a great choice for anyone who wants something focused on smart home control only. You can still ask Alexa questions and even play music, but the thin speakers aren't worth playing music from. But you can tell your Echo Hub to play music on a different set of speakers, and even set up default speakers to work with it. It's a great companion device if you already have a smart home setup.

Amazon Echo Pop: The Echo Pop is a perfectly fine little speaker, and the cutest one in Amazon's lineup. Does it have great sound? No. It's fine enough for background tunes or if you're limited to a dorm room, but you'll get much better sound for a similar size from the Echo Dot (but you'll pay a little more, and you won't get as cute of colors). It looks like Amazon has it fully out of stock, though, and only Best Buy seems to be carrying it right now, for twice the usual $40 price.

Amazon Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen) for $100: This smart display is another just-fine option, but it's too small to be a great display, and the included camera makes it a no for a bedside table; better to go with the above Echo Spot or an Echo Dot. Amazon did raise the price by $10.

Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $200: I usually love an Echo Show 8, but this model didn't have the same sound quality as the older model. If you're going to get one of Amazon's new displays, you're better off getting the Echo Show 11 ($250) for the same experience with a slightly larger screen (while it's a 3-inch difference, it doesn't feel that big) and better sound. Amazon did raise the price by $20.

Amazon Echo Show 15 (2nd Gen) for $350: This smart display is good, but it clearly wants to double as a TV and isn't very good at it yet. I'm hoping we see better TV-related performance in the future to make it worth adding to a kitchen or office. It does a great job with widgets, though, thanks to the massive 15.6-inch screen. There's also the larger Echo Show 21 ($500), which is essentially the same thing but larger. Both of these large displays rose in price—the Show 15 went up $50, while the Show 21 went up $100.

JBL Authentics 200 for $200: This JBL smart speaker supports both Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa, letting you switch between them for different tasks without changing your preference in the app. That makes this speaker particularly appealing for folks with a sprawling collection of smart products from both.

Sonos Era 100 for $219: If you're looking for a speaker that can talk to Alexa but isn't necessarily made by Amazon, the Sonos Era 100 is a great option. We just wish we liked the Sonos app better. You can catch our entire guide to the Sonos ecosystem here.

Amazon announced several new Echo models at the end of October that promise a richer Alexa+ experience. Some of these are new models of Echo speakers we've seen before, and some are entirely new. Here are all the new models, prices, and their standout features I'll be testing:

There's also the Alexa Photo Frame ($230), which will be a digital photo frame with Alexa+ built in. I haven't loved Amazon's past photo uploading experience for making its smart displays into photo frames, but I'll be testing it soon to see what the experience is like for a dedicated photo device. You'll be able to command Alexa+ on this device, but I hesitate to call it a speaker, since it doesn't sound designed for listening to music. Still, it's one of the new Alexa devices I'm most intrigued by, and it's available now.

Amazon raised many of its prices in August on its products, affecting the Amazon Echo line as well as Kindles, Fire TV streaming sticks, and Eero routers. It wasn't a huge surprise, as many companies have done this recently, citing rising costs and chip shortages, but this price hike happened ahead of Amazon launching new lines for most of these products, so it was likely to establish higher prices for the new lineup. Still, it's disappointing to see and will lead to a fall sale season with prices that won't be as impressive as earlier this summer.

Amazon's Echo devices saw increases from anywhere between $20 and $100, with the larger price increases being for the Echo Shows. The following Echo speakers all faced a price increase:

Amazon has rolled out the new-and-improved Amazon Alexa, named Alexa+, which is built on generative AI and promises a more powerful assistant that can handle more conversational topics and requests. It's available for a free 30-day trial; after that, you either pay a $20 monthly fee or become a Prime member. Being a Prime member is the better deal, likely by design. Neither my colleagues nor I have been impressed enough by Alexa+ to say it's worth paying for on its own. I do like the updated, more conversational voice, and Alexa+ did a good job answering all kinds of questions quickly and thoughtfully. Check out our early access hands-on for everything I thought while testing.

What’s the Difference Between an Echo and an Echo Show?

The best time to buy any Amazon speaker is during a major sale event like Black Friday or Amazon Prime Day, when there are often steep discounts. You'll often see the cheaper speakers for around 50 percent off, and the larger speakers see some nice sale prices, too.

How and Where Should You Set Up Your Alexa?

Ultimately, what's most important is that the speaker is somewhere it can hear your commands. Where that will be will vary based on your home, but think about where you'll be when you ask for the weather or to dim the lights, and place your speaker accordingly.

You'll set up Alexa speakers using the Alexa app, which allows you to manage multiple Alexa speakers linked to your Amazon account. Third-party speaker setup methods may vary.

Alexa is always listening, to a certain extent. It's designed to only listen for its wake word and shouldn't be recording or processing any audio unless it hears that word. But Alexa can sometimes mishear a word and think it's the wake word, or it might hear a word similar enough to activate the speaker. If you've owned an Alexa, there have likely been times when the assistant suddenly responds when you weren't speaking to it. Once it hears the wake word (or what it believes to be the wake word), it will start listening to everything in an attempt to hear what you need and respond.

Alexa+, the latest version of Alexa, will also remain on for a little bit after you ask a question to listen for follow-up questions, no wake word required. Both Alexa and Alexa+ light up in some fashion (regular speakers will turn the light ring blue, while the displays will have a blue bar appear on the screen) to let you know the assistant is listening. Most Echo devices also have a physical mute button and will display a red light or red bar to let you know when the mute is activated.

How Do You Remove Unwanted Content From an Echo Show?

If you're using an Echo Show device, you've likely noticed there is a ton of default content the device will show you. Sports scores! Local news! A recipe you might be interested in! It makes the device exhausting and annoying to be near.

Can I Have My Alexa Requests Locally Processed, or Do They Have to Go to the Cloud?

How Does WIRED Select Smart Speakers to Test? How Are These Speakers Tested?

For this guide, we specifically test speakers that are compatible with Amazon Alexa. It's a big limitation and narrows down the options significantly, especially compared to speaker options you'll see in our other guides like the Best Bluetooth Speakers. That's mainly Amazon's own ecosystem of speakers, and while there are third-party options, the best options tend to be of Amazon's own design to work with its own voice assistant.

Each speaker gets installed in a tester's home for day-to-day use, to see how the microphone performs, how the speaker sounds with different types of music, how well the smart home control features work with compatible devices such as smart lights and video doorbells, and to test other features as necessary (e.g., streaming features on smart displays).

How Does WIRED Get Models? What Does WIRED Do After Testing Them?

We usually obtain review units as press samples, though we will also independently purchase samples if need be. Any units were provided with no obligation to cover or promises for what that coverage would be.

After testing, we keep most of our picks either installed for long-term testing in our homes or in storage to compare against updated models and new speakers that come out. If the sample becomes irrelevant or unnecessary to keep, we donate it locally.
